On modern processors floating‑point numbers are represented in binary form according to the IEEE 754 standard. Each real value is stored as a finite number of bits that encode a sign bit, an exponent field and a fraction (mantissa). Because this representation can only hold about fifteen or sixteen decimal digits of precision for double‑precision values, many real numbers must be rounded to fit into the available mantissa bits. When two such rounded numbers are added, the exact mathematical sum is first computed in infinite precision, then the result is rounded again to conform to the same limited format. The rounding step introduces a tiny error that depends on the magnitude of the operands and on their binary alignment.

The IEEE 754 standard requires that each arithmetic operation be performed as if it were carried out with an infinitely precise intermediate result before being rounded once at the end of the instruction. This rule guarantees that the hardware behaves predictably for single operations, but it also means that the order in which operations are grouped can change the intermediate rounding points. For example, consider three numbers a, b and c whose pairwise sums differ slightly from their exact sum because of rounding. If one first adds a and b then rounds the result before adding c, the final rounded value may be different from the value obtained by first adding b and c and then adding a. The difference arises because each addition has its own round‑off error, and these errors do not cancel symmetrically when regrouped. Hence floating‑point addition is mathematically non‑associative on real hardware.

When large matrix multiplications are carried out, the total operation count can reach billions of additions and multiplications. In many high‑performance computing libraries the accumulation of partial products uses reduction trees: a binary tree structure that specifies an order in which pairwise sums are combined. The shape of this tree is dictated by factors such as cache size, vector width, or parallelism constraints. Because addition is non‑associative, different reduction orders produce slightly different rounding errors at each node of the tree. As the computation proceeds, these small discrepancies can propagate and magnify through subsequent operations. Even if every multiplication is performed exactly in hardware, the final sum of millions of partial products may drift by a few units in the last place (ULPs) from one reduction order to another.

This sensitivity has practical consequences for reproducibility. Two runs of the same matrix product on identical data but with different scheduling or parallelization can yield results that differ at the least significant bits. For many scientific applications this is acceptable, as the relative error remains far below the machine epsilon. However, in contexts where bit‑wise deterministic output is required—such as regression testing, cryptographic protocols, or reproducible research—the non‑associativity of floating‑point addition becomes a source of nondeterminism. Even subtle changes in compiler optimization flags, thread scheduling, or hardware microarchitecture can alter the reduction tree and thereby change the final binary representation of the result.

To mitigate these effects, developers sometimes enforce strict ordering by using higher precision accumulators (e.g., double‑double or quadruple precision), employ compensated summation algorithms like Kahan’s method, or adopt deterministic parallel reduction schemes that guarantee a fixed sequence of operations. Nonetheless, the fundamental limitation remains: because floating‑point addition is not mathematically associative on modern hardware, large matrix multiplications cannot be expected to produce identical bit patterns across all execution environments without additional precautions.

On modern processors floating‑point numbers are represented in binary according to the IEEE 754 standard, which stores each value as a sign bit, an exponent field and a fraction (mantissa) field with only 24 or 53 bits of precision for single and double formats respectively. When two such numbers are added, the hardware aligns their exponents, adds the significands, normalises the result, and finally rounds it to fit back into the limited mantissa. This rounding step discards any bits beyond the available precision; the discarded part is called the truncation error or round‑off error.

Because the rounding operation depends on the magnitude of the operands, the act of adding three numbers a, b and c in different groupings can produce slightly different results. If we compute (a + b) + c, the first addition produces an intermediate rounded value that may be close to a + b but not exact; when this rounded sum is added to c, the exponent alignment step may shift bits differently than if we had first computed b + c. The second grouping, a + (b + c), therefore yields a different final rounded result. In precise mathematical terms, the floating‑point addition operation is not associative: (a ⊕ b) ⊕ c ≠ a ⊕ (b ⊕ c) in general, where ⊕ denotes IEEE rounding.

Modern hardware implements this by performing each binary arithmetic instruction as an atomic operation with its own round‑off. Even the most sophisticated CPUs do not try to keep intermediate results at higher precision unless explicitly requested (e.g., using extended registers). Consequently, a single addition on one thread may produce a different rounded value from the same addition executed on another thread or in a different order because the sequence of exponent alignments and rounding decisions changes.

When large matrix multiplications are carried out, the operation reduces to thousands or millions of such elementary additions. Typically the product is accumulated by summing partial products across rows, columns or tiles. The reduction order—whether we sum along rows first, then columns, or interleave them—directly determines which intermediate rounded values are produced and how many times each rounding error occurs. If two runs use different loop orders or parallel reductions that combine results in distinct pairings, the final matrix entries can differ by a few units in the last place (ULPs). Though these differences may be minuscule relative to the magnitude of the numbers, they become significant when the computation is part of a larger algorithm where small perturbations can propagate, or when reproducibility across runs is required for debugging or scientific verification.

Moreover, many high‑performance libraries use hierarchical reductions or tree‑based accumulation to reduce memory traffic and exploit SIMD units. The shape of this reduction tree influences which partial sums are merged first; deeper trees may introduce more rounding operations because each merge step produces a rounded intermediate that will be used in subsequent merges. In practice, the same matrix multiplication executed on different numbers of threads, or with different compiler optimisations, can produce slightly different results simply because the hardware performs the additions in a different sequence.

Thus, the fundamental lack of associativity in floating‑point addition, together with the way modern processors handle rounding and parallel reductions, makes it impossible to guarantee identical outcomes for large matrix multiplications across varying reduction orders. Ensuring reproducibility requires either strict control over the exact order of operations—often at the cost of performance—or adopting numerically stable accumulation schemes such as Kahan summation or pairwise summation that minimise the impact of rounding errors.

Floating‑point addition on modern processors is not mathematically associative because of the way numbers are represented and rounded in binary format. IEEE 754 floating‑point arithmetic stores real values as a fixed‑width significand (mantissa) and an exponent. When two operands are added, the hardware aligns their exponents, adds the mantissas, and then rounds the result to fit back into the allotted precision. This rounding step discards bits that do not fit in the significand, producing a small but unavoidable error. If we add three numbers a, b, and c, performing (a + b) first will incur one rounding after adding a and b. The intermediate sum may have lost some low‑order bits. Adding c to this rounded value then produces another rounding that is influenced by the earlier loss. Conversely, if we compute (b + c) first, the initial rounding occurs on different operands, potentially preserving different low‑order bits, and when a is added afterwards the second rounding behaves differently. Because each addition’s rounding depends on the exact binary representation of its inputs, the two sequences can yield results that differ in the last few bits, even though mathematically they should be equal.

Modern CPUs also introduce additional non‑associativity through fused multiply–add (FMA) instructions and extended precision registers. An FMA performs a multiplication followed immediately by an addition with only one rounding at the end of the entire operation, which can produce more accurate results than performing the multiplication and addition separately. If some parts of a computation use FMA while others do not—perhaps due to compiler optimizations or different instruction sets—the relative error pattern changes further. Moreover, most processors keep intermediate results in floating‑point registers that may have 80 bits of precision (x87) or 64 bits (AVX), but when the result is stored back into memory it is rounded again to the target format (typically 32 or 64 bits). The path from register to memory introduces yet another rounding, and whether a value goes through an extended‑precision register before being written out can depend on compiler decisions or vector length.

When large matrix multiplications are performed, each output element is computed as a dot product: a sum of many products. The reduction order—the sequence in which partial sums are combined—determines how rounding errors accumulate. If the algorithm uses a simple left‑to‑right accumulation, early terms may dominate and later small terms might be lost due to rounding. A more balanced binary tree reduction spreads the error more evenly but can still result in different intermediate values depending on the exact pairing of terms. Modern parallel implementations often use tree reductions across threads or vector lanes; each thread may follow a slightly different schedule, leading to a different sequence of additions. Even if two runs compute the same mathematical matrix product, differences in thread scheduling, cache behavior, or instruction reordering can cause the reduction tree to differ subtly. Consequently, the final matrices produced on two separate executions can diverge by one or more units in the last place (ULP), especially for large dimensions where millions of additions are involved.

This lack of associativity undermines reproducibility: scientific simulations that rely on deterministic outputs may observe small discrepancies when run on different machines or even on the same machine at different times. Debugging such differences is challenging because they are often invisible in high‑level code but rooted in low‑level hardware behavior. Some strategies to mitigate the issue include using compensated summation algorithms (Kahan, Neumaier), enforcing a fixed reduction order, or performing computations in higher precision and only rounding at the end. Nonetheless, the fundamental non‑associativity of floating‑point addition on modern hardware ensures that perfect reproducibility across all platforms is generally unattainable without explicit control over every arithmetic operation’s ordering and precision.

Floating‑point arithmetic on modern processors follows the IEEE‑754 standard, which specifies that each operation produces a result rounded to the nearest representable value in the chosen precision. This rounding step introduces a small error that depends on the exact operands and the intermediate results. Because the rounding is performed after every binary operation, the sequence of operations matters: if two numbers are added first and then the sum is added to a third number, the intermediate result will be rounded once before it participates in the next addition. If instead the second and third numbers are added first, the rounding occurs at a different point, producing a slightly different intermediate value. The difference between these two paths can be as large as one unit in the last place (ULP) of the final result, which is why floating‑point addition is not mathematically associative on hardware.

The lack of associativity becomes especially problematic when performing large matrix multiplications. A typical matrix product involves summing many products of individual elements: each entry of the result matrix is a dot product of two vectors, and the overall multiplication can be viewed as a series of inner‑product reductions followed by accumulation into the output matrix. In practice, high‑performance libraries such as BLAS or vendor‑specific kernels use various reduction trees to exploit parallelism and cache locality. Some implementations perform pairwise summation in a balanced binary tree, while others accumulate results sequentially or use blocking strategies that change the order of addition across threads.

Because each different reduction tree changes the sequence of rounding operations, the final accumulated values can differ by small amounts. In many applications these differences are negligible compared to the magnitude of the numbers involved, but for numerically sensitive problems they can propagate and amplify through subsequent computations. When a matrix multiplication is repeated on two machines with slightly different instruction sets or compiler optimizations, the chosen reduction order may vary even if the source code is identical. The resulting outputs will then differ in the last few bits, leading to reproducibility issues: running the same algorithm twice under ostensibly identical conditions can produce distinct floating‑point results.

The effect is compounded when matrices are large and dense. Each entry requires thousands or millions of multiplications and additions; a tiny rounding error at each step accumulates across many operations. Even if the relative error per operation is on the order of 10⁻¹⁶, after tens of thousands of steps the cumulative deviation can reach 10⁻¹² or more. In scientific simulations, machine learning training, or financial modeling, such discrepancies may alter convergence behavior, change classification outcomes, or affect risk estimates.

To mitigate these issues, developers sometimes enforce a fixed reduction order by using deterministic algorithms, such as Kahan summation or pairwise summation with a prescribed tree structure. Some libraries provide “reproducible” modes that serialize operations or use higher precision accumulators to reduce variability. However, enforcing strict associativity often comes at the cost of performance because it limits parallelism and cache efficiency. Consequently, practitioners must balance reproducibility against speed, carefully documenting the reduction strategy used so that results can be compared across different runs or platforms.

In floating‑point arithmetic the values that a computer can represent are only approximations of real numbers. A finite binary format stores a sign bit, an exponent field, and a fraction (mantissa) that is rounded to a fixed number of bits. When two numbers are added the exact mathematical sum may not be exactly representable in this format, so the result must be rounded to the nearest representable value according to a chosen rounding mode. This rounding step introduces a tiny error, called round‑off.

The associative law states that (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c). In exact real arithmetic it holds true because addition is mathematically associative. With floating point, however, the two different parenthesizations involve different intermediate results and therefore different rounding operations. Suppose we add three numbers whose pairwise sums lie just below or above a representable boundary. Adding the first two may round one way, producing an intermediate that when added to the third rounds differently than if we had rounded after adding the second pair first. The difference between the two final results is typically on the order of a few units in the last place (ULPs), but it can be significant for large computations where many such small errors accumulate.

On modern hardware, floating‑point addition is usually implemented with fused operations that may also involve extra precision registers or intermediate rounding to avoid overflow and underflow. The exact sequence of rounding can depend on compiler optimizations, instruction scheduling, and the presence of fused multiply‑add units. Consequently, even adding the same three numbers in the same order but compiled differently or executed on different CPUs can yield slightly different results.

When a large matrix multiplication is performed, each element of the result matrix is computed as a dot product: a sum over many products of corresponding entries. The reduction (accumulation) order for that sum is not fixed; it depends on how the algorithm iterates through indices and how the compiler schedules loops. Two executions with different loop orders or different blocking strategies will therefore accumulate partial sums in a different sequence, causing each element to be subject to a distinct pattern of rounding errors. Because these small differences are not guaranteed to cancel out, the final matrix can differ by a few ULPs per entry.

In practice, for very large matrices or when many multiplications are chained together—such as in deep learning training or scientific simulations—even tiny discrepancies can grow into noticeable divergences. This lack of strict reproducibility has prompted the development of algorithms that use compensated summation (e.g., Kahan sum) or higher precision accumulators to reduce sensitivity to reduction order, and it also motivates hardware support for deterministic floating‑point operations in some high‑performance computing contexts. Nonetheless, because the associativity property fails at the machine level, any algorithm that relies on a particular accumulation pattern cannot guarantee identical results across different runs unless additional precautions are taken.

On modern processors floating‑point addition is performed in a finite, fixed precision format defined by the IEEE 754 standard, typically binary64 (double precision). The hardware represents numbers as a significand and an exponent; when two numbers are added the result is computed exactly in principle, but it must be rounded to fit back into the available bits. Rounding introduces an error that depends on the magnitude of the operands and on how close their sum is to a representable value. Because this rounding error is generally non‑zero, the operation \(a + (b + c)\) can give a different result from \((a + b) + c\). The difference arises because each grouping forces a distinct intermediate rounding: in the first case the pair \(b + c\) is rounded before adding to \(a\); in the second case \(a + b\) is rounded first. If the errors happen to cancel or amplify depending on the order, the final result will differ by one or more units in the last place (ULPs). This non‑associativity is inherent to floating point and cannot be eliminated by software; it is a consequence of finite precision arithmetic.

Modern CPUs often include fused multiply–add (FMA) instructions that compute \(a \times b + c\) with only one rounding, instead of two. While FMA can reduce error compared with separate mul and add operations, the reduction still depends on the order in which terms are grouped. When a matrix multiplication is carried out by summing many products, the algorithm typically performs an accumulation over one dimension (e.g., rows or columns). Different software libraries choose different reduction trees: some use a simple left‑to‑right loop, others interleave partial sums in a tree or pairwise fashion to reduce rounding error. In a left‑to‑right accumulation each new product is added to the running total, causing every addition to be rounded once. A tree‑structured reduction adds pairs of partial sums first, halving the number of terms at each level, and can change both the sequence of rounding operations and the magnitudes of intermediate results. Because the rounding error at each step depends on the current accumulator value, a different order changes the distribution of errors across the computation.

When large matrices are multiplied on multi‑core or many‑threaded systems, the situation becomes even more pronounced. Each thread may compute partial sums independently; later these partial sums are combined. The interleaving of operations from different threads introduces nondeterminism in the exact sequence of additions. Even if two runs use identical code, factors such as thread scheduling, cache state, or instruction reordering by the compiler can alter which pairings occur first. Consequently, a single matrix product may produce slightly different results depending on the reduction strategy and runtime conditions. For applications that demand strict reproducibility—such as scientific simulations, financial risk models, or benchmarking—the cumulative effect of these small differences can lead to noticeable discrepancies in final outputs.

Practitioners sometimes mitigate this by enforcing a fixed summation order (e.g., using a deterministic tree), employing higher precision accumulators like Kahan summation, or performing all operations in extended precision and rounding only at the end. However, these approaches increase computational cost or complexity. In many large‑scale computing environments, reproducibility is traded off against performance, accepting that floating‑point arithmetic will not be perfectly associative on modern hardware.

Floating‑point arithmetic in contemporary processors follows the IEEE 754 standard, which specifies a finite binary representation for real numbers. Each number is stored as a sign bit, an exponent field, and a fraction (mantissa). The exponent determines the scale while the mantissa holds only a fixed amount of significant bits—typically 24 for single precision or 53 for double precision. Because this representation can describe only about six to fifteen decimal digits accurately, numbers that would be representable in exact mathematics must be rounded to fit into the available bit width.

When two floating‑point operands are added, the processor aligns their exponents so that the least significant bits line up before performing a binary addition of the mantissas. The result is then rounded back to the nearest representable value according to the selected rounding mode (usually “round toward nearest, ties to even”). This round‑off introduces an error bounded by one unit in the last place (ULP). In exact arithmetic, the sum of two numbers is unique and addition is associative: (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c). In floating‑point, however, the rounding after each addition can produce different intermediate results, so associativity fails. If a + b produces a value that must be rounded down, but b + c produces a value that rounds up, the final sums will differ by more than one ULP. The difference is amplified if the operands have very different magnitudes; aligning exponents may discard many low‑order bits of the smaller operand, causing a larger loss in precision.

Modern CPUs also employ various optimizations that exacerbate non‑associativity. Many cores perform fused multiply–add (FMA) operations, which compute a*b + c with only one rounding step, yielding higher accuracy than separate multiplication and addition. Other microarchitectural features such as out‑of‑order execution, speculative loads, vector instructions, or the use of extended precision registers in the floating‑point unit can change the order in which partial results are produced and rounded. Even when the same mathematical expression is executed on identical hardware, different compiler optimizations or scheduling decisions may alter the reduction tree used to combine intermediate sums.

Large matrix multiplications rely on summing many products across rows and columns. The natural algorithm computes each entry as a dot product: for fixed indices i and j it adds up n terms of the form A[i,k] * B[k,j]. In practice, the accumulation is performed with an associative reduction tree whose shape depends on loop ordering, vector width, or parallelism. If two runs use different reduction orders—say one sums left‑to‑right while another balances the tree—the intermediate partial sums will be rounded differently at each stage. Because each rounding error can drift a few ULPs, the final entries may differ by several ULPs as well. In large matrices, these small per‑element discrepancies accumulate into noticeable differences in norms or condition numbers.

The lack of associativity thus undermines reproducibility: identical high‑level code run on the same hardware but with different compiler flags, thread scheduling, or instruction ordering can produce outputs that differ beyond machine epsilon. For scientific applications where deterministic results are essential—such as verification tests, iterative solvers, or reproducible research—this variability is problematic. One mitigation strategy is to enforce strict accumulation order using higher precision accumulators (e.g., double‑extended) or software techniques like Kahan summation, but these come at a performance cost. Another approach is to use deterministic reduction trees and avoid vectorized FMA when exact reproducibility across runs is required. Understanding that floating‑point addition is not associative on modern hardware explains why seemingly minor changes in computation order can lead to measurable differences in large matrix multiplications.
